items.title: Anthropic IPO: four ways the AI giant wants to disrupt science
items.summary: The firm aims to cure diseases, accelerate discovery and automate science — but many researchers are sceptical of its lofty ambitions.

items.title: Mathematicians astounded by AI and human-written proofs of iconic Riemann hypothesis
items.summary: Scholars say that the rival claims to have derived a proof for a landmark problem in mathematics will need rigorous checking.

items.title: More tropical cyclones hit peak fury at the worst possible time
items.summary: Climate change is creating conditions that pump up the intensity of hurricanes and typhoons just as the storms reach the coast.

items.title: How to make AI data centres more sustainable
items.summary: Tech companies and governments face opposition over data centres’ expansion, in part because of their huge power requirements. They must not be powered with fossil fuels.

items.title: BepiColombo finally reaches Mercury after eight-year odyssey
items.summary: European and Japanese probes will trace different paths around the planet to study its surface and its surroundings.

items.title: Net zero emissions won’t reverse climate change — some nations look to ‘net negative’
items.summary: Countries are starting to grapple with the reality that bringing temperatures down after they breach the 1.5 ºC target would require removing massive amounts of carbon dioxide from the air.

items.title: AI is turbocharging cyberattacks — can computer scientists catch up?
items.summary: Cybersecurity researchers who don’t use the technology for spotting software bugs now 'risk falling behind'.

items.title: AI is ditching hallucinated references — and other bad habits
items.summary: An analysis finds that many undesirable LLM behaviours dissipate after about 16 months.

items.title: These gaps in weather data affect forecasts everywhere: plugging them is not charity
items.summary: Investing in observations in low-income countries will help to prevent climate disasters worldwide.

items.title: Claude, find me a planet: amateur astronomers are using AI with mixed results
items.summary: Artificial-intelligence tools are helping citizen scientists to identify previously unknown exoplanet candidates — some more credible than others.

items.title: Briefing Chat: Voyager 1 is now one ‘light day’ from Earth — setting a cosmic record
items.summary: Nature staff discuss the probe’s epic journey — plus, how vampire bats survive on a blood-only diet.

items.title: People entering old age now have better memory than their parents did
items.summary: Older people today maintain memory function for longer than previous generations did, according to a study of 219,000 adults.

items.title: Sore throat? The brain has surprising control over how ill you feel
items.summary: The brain might decode pathogens, store memories of previous illnesses and prepare the body for future threats.

items.title: Glucose-powered implant brings devices for treating diabetes a step closer
items.summary: A device that stimulates the main nerve between the brain and the internal organs when blood sugar is high is an effective therapy in rat models of diabetes.

items.title: Sleuth finds ‘impossible proteins’ in hundreds of research papers
items.summary: Investigation exposes a potentially widespread problem, prompting retractions and corrections.

items.title: Lifting weights reduces muscle loss from obesity drugs
items.summary: Resistance exercise could help middle-aged and older individuals to maintain muscle mass and strength during weight-loss treatment.

items.title: First observation of a giant star swallowing its neighbour
items.summary: Finding provides new insights into what happens within stellar mergers — plus, using quantum physics to securely pinpoint someone’s location.

items.title: Tropical land-use intensification reshapes biodiversity in expected and unexpected ways
items.summary: Global agricultural demand has increased over the past few decades, driving land-use intensification in some of the world’s most biodiverse regions. An assessment of some 40,000 species, from soil microorganisms to vertebrates, in Sumatra, Indonesia, reveals that agricultural intensification threatens biodiversity through species loss and changes in community composition across different spatial scales.

items.title: Fraud helps little fire ants to survive and conquer
items.summary: Invasive ants in China overcome larger rivals with a crafty stratagem and vigorous attack.

items.title: What do various cancers have in common?
items.summary: An analysis of 42 cancer types reveals shared patterns of gene activity in the tumour microenvironment, which might point to treatments that work across a range of cancers.

items.title: Bacteria and viruses team up to hasten the demise of algal blooms
items.summary: Algal blooms are important ecological phenomena that drive carbon fixation and fuel the marine food web. Viral infection often ends them abruptly. Some bacteria can sense infected algal cells and then act in synergy with viruses to expedite a bloom’s collapse.

items.title: Intra-stellar: a star inside a giant star
items.summary: Long-term monitoring of a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy reveals, for the first time, the decay of the orbit of another star inside the giant’s envelope.

items.title: A new view of Amazonian leaf seasonality
items.summary: Much of the Amazon rainforest was thought to be evergreen, but high-resolution satellite imagery reveals that many of its trees can remain leafless for longer than expected.

items.title: AI must be held accountable — value statements won’t protect human dignity
items.summary: Technology companies can’t be the judges of their own regulatory compliance. Centuries of history explain why.

items.title: Widespread deciduousness reveals diverse Amazonian phenological strategies
items.summary: A basin-wide assessment of Amazonian deciduousness using high-resolution satellite observations shows a diverse range of phenological strategies across the Amazon rainforest, contrary to the prevailing view of Amazonian phenology.

items.title: US science academy urges journals to fix errors more quickly
items.summary: Long-awaited report makes recommendations for strengthening the reliability of the scientific record.

items.title: University students are biggest spreaders of COVID
items.summary: Undergraduates were the first group to spread genetic variants of SARS-CoV-2 during the pandemic, mega-analysis finds.

items.title: Daily briefing: Homo erectus had what it takes to thrive in the rainforest
items.summary: Fossil teeth suggest that Homo erectus could live in a habitat researchers thought that only Homo sapiens could hack. Plus, what experts think remains underappreciated in neuroscience and tips on networking at a conference.

items.title: Microbiome home tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?
items.summary: Our reporter mailed off her poo to find out what two companies say about her microbiome. Here’s what she found.

items.title: Kings of the jungle? This early human had surprising survival skills that rivalled ours
items.summary: Teeth found in south China challenge the idea that Homo erectus lived only in woodlands and on savannahs.

items.title: Poxviruses probably evolved in the digestive system of animals
items.summary: Large and giant DNA viruses that infect unicellular eukaryotes are abundant in the environment but have rarely been found in the gut microbiome. The discovery of such viruses that prevail in the digestive system of humans and animals exposes a long-overlooked facet of the gut microbiome that clarifies the origin of poxviruses.

items.title: Meet ‘egoviruses’: the surprise microbes living in the guts of millions of people
items.summary: Egoviruses could be the evolutionary missing link between giant viruses that infect single-celled organisms and those that can infect people.

items.title: Quantum physics can prove where you are
items.summary: Demonstrating your location to someone far away is surprisingly hard. Quantum correlations offer a way to do so without needing to trust any quantum hardware.

items.title: ‘I had felt overconfident’: senior scientists reveal mistakes that aided discovery
items.summary: Five experienced researchers, including a Nobel prizewinner, revisit the dead ends, bloopers and moments of stubborn certainty that shaped their science.

items.title: Injured locusts heal or are cannibalized depending on levels of a bacterial odour molecule
items.summary: When migratory locusts are injured, an odorous chemical produced by bacteria living in or on their bodies activates the immune system, helping them to fight disease-causing agents. However, when a wound is large and the chemical becomes too concentrated, it attracts cannibalistic locusts.

items.summary: Join a free webinar to discuss how the technology is changing researchers' roles, their skills and job security.

items.summary: A rapid microgrants scheme called the Field Building Accelerator aims to launch new scientific fields.

items.title: ‘Incredibly frustrating’: prestigious fellowship applications close in just 21 hours
items.summary: The Humboldt Foundation says that applications for its fellowships have increased markedly in the past two years, but they did not anticipate the influx this month.

items.summary: Take Nature’s quiz to test your skills as a research-integrity sleuth. Plus, a milestone for Voyager 1 and the United States has lost its measles elimination status.

items.title: How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower
items.summary: A nagging sense that you don’t belong can keep you grounded and might help to improve your performance.

items.summary: Sleuths and publishers seize on ‘tortured phrases’ to detect research fraud. Sometimes they can raise a smile.
